title: Global Ecology and Evolutionary Drivers of Spiny‐Trunk Trees
content:
ABSTRACT

Aim

Throughout the Cenozoic, herbivory by large mammals has shaped plant evolution, including plant defences such as spines. Trunk spines were recently identified as functionally distinct from leaf-defending spines, but their ecological function and evolutionary drivers remain unclear. We investigated their global distribution, ecology and potential drivers in woody plants.

Location

Global.

Time Period

Contemporary plant distributions; present-natural mammal distribution reconstructed over the past 130 kyr.

Major Taxa Studied

Angiosperms—Eudicots; herbivorous mammals > 5 kg.

Methods

We compiled a global dataset of 95 woody species with trunk spines and mapped both their absolute and relative richness. We quantified relative spiny-trunk richness across terrestrial biomes and ecoregions and used gradient-boosting models, with spatial block cross-validation and accumulated local effects, to assess associations with vegetation productivity and structure, climate seasonality and herbivory pressure, represented by present-natural mammal richness and modelled plant consumption. We also evaluated associations with the richness of individual mammal clades.

Results

Among occupied cells, relative spiny-trunk richness was highest in tropical and subtropical ecosystems combining high herbivory pressure, high productivity and pronounced dry-season deciduousness, particularly in seasonally flooded savannas and forest-grassland mosaics. Artiodactyla, Rodentia and Primates were the most consistently associated extant orders despite wide spatial uncertainty, while endemic American clades including mostly extinct large herbivores—Litopterna, Cingulata and Pilosa—were also prominent.

Main Conclusions

Trunk spines show a biogeographic pattern distinct from the predominantly arid distribution of leaf-defending spines. Their concentration in productive but strongly seasonal, herbivore-rich ecosystems is consistent with selection where seasonal resource bottlenecks may concentrate mammalian damage on woody trunks. Bark feeding provides the clearest functional hypothesis, while mechanical damage and climbing deterrence remain plausible. These patterns highlight the evolutionary legacy of large mammal herbivores and a potentially underappreciated role of non-foliar herbivory in shaping plant defence and vegetation structure.
